shots.narration: In Yellowstone,
bison have injured more people than any other animal, bears included.
By the end, Doug steps between two fighting bulls, each about as heavy as two grand pianos, to referee.
Winter.
The Wolves.
When Yellowstone's wolves hunt an elk,
adding more wolves stops helping once the pack has somewhere between two and six.
When they hunt a bison, it keeps helping until the pack reaches nine to thirteen wolves,
and possibly more.
That is a football team of predators, plus a substitute, for one animal that eats grass.
Elk are the wolves' main prey,
and the researchers who watched these hunts call bison the most difficult prey for wolves to kill in North America.
Wolves were brought back to the park in nineteen ninety-five,
and the first time anyone documented them bringing down an adult bison here was four years later.
Here's the part that should worry you.
A wolf that tries this on its own succeeds about once in every hundred tries,
and even a bison that has been caught and held often just gets away.
The top predator in the park only gets its best odds with about a dozen of itself,
and bison have killed wolves that tried.
So Doug is in a wolf costume, to make the numbers up.
The pack is twelve, and Doug is thirteen.
Doug did not agree to this.
The bison looks down the line of wolves
and picks the newest member.
Doug has died. Again.
And that was a bison barely trying,
because in winter it is busy doing something much stranger with its face.
The Snowplow.
A bison in winter gets to its dinner by swinging its whole head from side to side,
sweeping the snow away like a plow made of face.
That hump on its shoulders is not a fat store.
It is muscle, held up by long bones that rise from the backbone,
and it gives the neck and shoulders the power to swing a head that heavy all day.
A bull can weigh up to about nine hundred kilograms,
which is about the same as two concert grand pianos,
and a cow can weigh up to about half that.
In winter, plenty of the herd gather around the park's steaming thermal areas
and along the Madison River, and that is where they dig for grasses and sedges.
The unsettling thing about a winter bison is that it does not care about you at all.
It is not angry, and it is not hunting you, because it is busy.
Doug grabs a shovel to help,
and in the time it takes him to clear one step,
the bull clears a whole path
and then plows straight through Doug's pile.
Doug is fine.
The narrator had expected a lot more from this one.
The last bison Doug met had been dead for thirty-six thousand years,
and he ate some of it.
This one is less forgiving.
That swing moves a lot of snow, and the same head and neck are what a bison uses on people.
The Hump.
The muscles that shovel snow all winter are the same ones a bison uses when it charges,
and the head on the end of them comes with horns.
Both males and females have short horns that curve upward,
and a male's are only slightly longer on average,
so there is no safe half of the herd.
When park researchers went through sixteen years of bison injuries,
they sorted them into three kinds.
The bison butts with its head,
hooks with a horn,
or throws the person into the air.
Twelve of the twenty-five people in that study ended up in hospital.
That last one works like a forklift that lifts and flicks in a single move.
And this is the bit that matters.
Nothing about the charge is a new skill,
because everything a bison does to get through the winter is practice for it.
Doug is standing exactly where the head is about to swing next,
which is where the snow used to be.
Doug goes up,
and he does not come back down in this shot.
Doug has died. Again.
Winter was the easy part,
because in spring the herd gets something new to protect, and it is small and orange.
Spring.
The Calf.
Within about thirty minutes of being born, a bison calf can stand up and feed,
and within a couple of hours it is walking with the herd.
In Yellowstone the calves arrive in late April and May,
with an orange-brown to reddish coat, and people around the park call them red dogs.
A newborn weighs about fifteen to thirty kilograms,
roughly a checked suitcase at the airport limit,
and it lives surrounded by animals many times its size.
Here's the problem with calves.
In May twenty twenty-three, a calf was separated from its mother as the herd crossed a river,
and a visitor pushed it up out of the water and onto the road.
The herd would not take it back, and the calf died.
The smallest bison in the park is the one that gets people into trouble,
and sometimes the one that gets hurt.
The last time Doug saw a bison in trouble, he walked over to help and got stuck with it.
So this time, Doug sees a calf on its own and goes over to say hello.
The calf is not alone.
Doug has died. Again.
Its mother covered the distance before Doug had finished saying hello,
and she was nowhere near her top speed.
The Speed.
Something that looks like a sofa with a beard
can run at up to about fifty-five kilometers an hour.
At that speed, a bison crosses the whole length of a tennis court, baseline to baseline,
in about a second and a half.
A tennis court also happens to be almost exactly the distance the park asks people to keep from a bison.
It can also jump over things about one and a half meters high,
it is agile, and it is a strong swimmer.
The park's own fact sheet adds, plainly, that bison can be aggressive.
The worst part is how it looks the rest of the time.
A Yellowstone bison spends nine to eleven hours a day with its head down, eating,
and it looks like the least athletic animal in the park.
Nobody believes it can do this until it does.
So Doug is timing a bison with a stopwatch, for science,
and he has chosen to stand on the finish line so he gets the best view.
The bison finishes before Doug presses start.
Doug has died. Again.
So far, the bison has mostly been minding its own business,
but then summer arrives, and so do the visitors.
Summer.
The Record.
Since nineteen eighty, bison have injured more people walking around Yellowstone than any other animal in the park.
The park's rule is to stay at least twenty-three meters from a bison at all times,
which is about a quarter of an American football field.
Between May and July of twenty fifteen, five people were hurt by bison,
and every one of those incidents happened in a busy place, like a hiking trail or a geyser basin.
Three of them were taking photos,
and they were about one to two meters from the animal,
which is closer than people used to get back in the nineteen eighties and nineties.
From two thousand to twenty fifteen, the park counted twenty-five people hurt by bison,
and every one of them had been within about six meters of the animal beforehand.
But here's the strange thing about this record. Eight in ten of those people had walked up to the bison.

elements.text: 8 IN 10 HAD WALKED UP TO IT

shots.narration: The bison did not come to them.

shots.narration: Doug wants a photo with the record holder,
so he walks backwards toward it with a selfie stick, trying to fit it all in the frame.
The photo is great.
Doug has died. Again.
The bull went back to grazing,
and in summer the herd likes to graze its way right along the road.
The Jam.
In Yellowstone, a traffic jam often has a bison at the front of it,
walking down the middle of the road at whatever speed it likes.
Herds walk along and across the park roads,
especially in late summer, when the herds move into the Lamar and Hayden valleys.
The danger runs both ways.
In twenty eighteen, park data counted twenty-five bison killed by vehicles on park roads,
which was more than any other large animal that year.
Drivers killed seventy-six large animals on park roads in total,
so bison were about a third of them.
Twenty-five in a year is about one bison every two weeks, as regular as a fortnightly paycheck.
And in August twenty twenty-two, at the height of the mating season,
a bison walked up to a car stuck in a jam and rammed it with its head.
Nobody had even stepped outside.
The part nobody puts on a sign is who has right of way.
In Yellowstone it is the bison, and nobody gave it to them.
They took it.
Doug gets out of his car to move them along,
with a big friendly wave, because he has somewhere to be.
Doug has died. Again.
The herd is still in the road.
By late July, the bulls have almost stopped caring about cars, or grass, or anything at all except each other.
The rut.
The Wallow.
In August, dust clouds rise over the valleys,
and the dust is coming from bison throwing themselves onto the ground.
Bison roll in the dirt all year round.
It is called wallowing, and it helps keep biting flies away and rubs off old tufts of winter fur.
In the rut, which here runs from late July through August,
the bulls wallow far more often, and they roll violently on the ground to show how aggressive they are.
They bellow too, and the deep bellow of a bull can be heard right across the landscape, which is the point.
The park says bulls show high amounts of aggression during the rut.
Picture a dog rolling on the rug,
then scale the dog up to nine hundred kilograms and put it in a very bad mood.
The thing to understand about that dust cloud on the horizon is that it is not weather.
It is a crowd of very large animals, all angry with each other.
Doug rolls in a wallow as well, to fit in.
A bull watches him for a while,
decides that Doug is not competition,
and leaves.
Doug is fine.
The narrator finds this result insulting, on Doug's behalf.
That bull had somewhere more important to be, because a rival on the far side of the valley had just bellowed back.
The Rut.
During the rut, a bull can lose almost ninety kilograms,
about one whole Doug, because he barely stops to eat.
That is about twelve percent of his body weight, spent on guarding, bellowing, and fighting.
When he finds a cow who is nearly ready to mate, he stays right beside her
for anywhere from a few minutes to a few days.
Rival bulls get bellows, wallowing and threats.
If the threats fail,
the two bulls lock horns and shove each other back and forth,
kicking up dust across the valley.
There are a lot of bulls to do this.
Yellowstone is the only place in the United States where bison have lived since prehistoric times,
and poachers cut the herd to about two dozen by nineteen oh two.
In twenty twenty-five there were nearly five thousand three hundred.
And to be fair to the bison, they very rarely kill anyone.
From two thousand to twenty fifteen, bison hurt twenty-five people in the park, and none of them died.
Bears have killed more people here than bison have.
The bison holds the injury record because so many people walk up to it.
Which brings us to the referee.
Two bulls, each about as heavy as two grand pianos, square up in the dust,
and Doug steps into the gap between them with a whistle.
Doug blows the whistle.
Both bulls charge at the same moment,
and Doug is the only thing either of them hits.
Doug has died. Again.
The narrator has added a sticky note to the field guide,
and all it says is plant eater.
The cap has been adopted by the herd,
and from now on, it has right of way.
Doug deaths: two hundred and seventy-four.
Seven of them from a plant eater.
The next place Doug isn't welcome is on your screen now.
